# ECS, EKS, Fargate and ECR: say it

<!-- speak:start id=containers-s01 -->
### Prompt 1

**A customer asks.** ECS or EKS? My one Kubernetes engineer says that EKS is the standard.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Both run your containers, and both work with Fargate. EKS fits teams that already run Kubernetes. With ECS, you have less to run yourself.

**In 60 seconds.**

Both run your containers, and both can run them on Fargate, with no servers to manage.

The difference is who you need on the team.

It works like this. Amazon ECS is the AWS orchestrator, with no extra charge for ECS itself.

You describe each service in a task definition, and AWS runs it.

Amazon EKS runs open-source Kubernetes, so your existing Kubernetes tools and plug-ins work.

AWS runs the Kubernetes control plane for you, and each cluster has an hourly fee.

The thing to watch is the upgrades.

Kubernetes clusters need frequent upgrades, and someone on your team has to run them.

In your case, you plan six services and you have one Kubernetes engineer.

I'd start on ECS with Fargate, and keep EKS for when the team grows.

Who would run the cluster upgrades if your Kubernetes engineer is away?

**Skeleton.** both run on Fargate / ECS: no extra charge / EKS: open-source Kubernetes, hourly fee / upgrades need Kubernetes skills

**Must say.**

- Both Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS can run their containers on AWS Fargate.
- EKS runs open-source Kubernetes, so existing Kubernetes plug-ins and tooling work.
- Every EKS cluster has a per cluster per hour fee; Amazon ECS itself has no additional charge.
- The skills of the organization are a major factor: teams that run Kubernetes handle frequent cluster upgrades.

**Do not say.**

- "ECS is not for production; EKS is the standard on AWS.". Say: Amazon ECS is a fully managed container orchestration service to deploy, manage and scale containerized applications.
- "With EKS we would run the Kubernetes control plane ourselves.". Say: AWS manages the EKS control plane for you and makes it available across Availability Zones.
- "EKS costs nothing extra, the same as ECS.". Say: All Amazon EKS clusters have a per cluster per hour fee.

**Follow-up questions.**

- Can we move from ECS to EKS later? Yes. Amazon ECR works with both Amazon ECS and Amazon EKS, so the same images stay. You rewrite the task definitions as Kubernetes manifests.
- Can EKS use Fargate Spot to save money? No. Amazon EKS doesn't support Fargate Spot. For Spot capacity on EKS, use a managed node group with the Spot capacity type.

</details>
<!-- speak:end -->

<!-- speak:start id=containers-s02 -->
### Prompt 2

**A customer asks.** Should we run our containers on Fargate or on EC2 instances? We want low cost and little operations work.

<details>
<summary>Answer</summary>

**In 10 seconds.** Start on Fargate: no instances to manage, and you pay per second for each task's size. Use EC2 for GPUs or large, price-optimized fleets.

**In 60 seconds.**

The short answer is: start on Fargate, and move to EC2 when a workload needs it.

It works like this. On Fargate, you don't choose, patch or scale any instances.

Each task asks for vCPU and memory, and you pay for that, per second.

You pay for what you provision, even when the task is idle.

On EC2, you manage the instances, but you get root access and GPUs.

For large fleets where price matters most, AWS suggests EC2 capacity.

ECS Managed Instances is a middle path: AWS patches them, and GPUs work.

The thing to watch is how you lower the Fargate bill.

Fargate Spot is cheaper for tasks that can be interrupted.

Compute Savings Plans also apply to Fargate usage.

In your case, I'd put every service on Fargate first.

Do any of your containers need a GPU or access to the host?

**Skeleton.** Fargate first, EC2 when needed / pay per second for size / EC2: control, GPUs, large fleets / Spot and Savings Plans lower bill

**Must say.**

- With Fargate you no longer provision, configure, or scale clusters of virtual machines to run containers.
- Fargate bills the vCPU and memory that a task requests, from the image pull until the task stops, rounded up to the nearest second.
- EC2 capacity fits large workloads that must be price optimized, and GPU workloads, which Fargate does not support today.
- Fargate Spot gives a discount for interruption-tolerant tasks, and Compute Savings Plans apply to Fargate usage.

**Do not say.**

- "Fargate always costs more than EC2.". Say: On Fargate you pay for what you provision, so compare the real task sizes with well-used instances.
- "Fargate can run our GPU jobs too.". Say: GPU workloads are not supported on AWS Fargate today. Run them on Amazon EC2.
- "When Spot capacity runs out, Fargate Spot starts the tasks on regular Fargate.". Say: Fargate doesn't replace Spot capacity with on-demand capacity. Give the FARGATE capacity provider a base for the tasks that must keep running.

**Follow-up questions.**

- What happens when AWS takes a Fargate Spot task back? The task gets a two-minute warning, sent as a SIGTERM signal to the task and as an event to Amazon EventBridge. The container must handle SIGTERM and save its work, or data can be lost.
- Does a Savings Plan cover Fargate? Compute Savings Plans do: they also apply to Fargate and Lambda usage. EC2 Instance Savings Plans apply to one instance family in one Region.

</details>
